t: The wall speech in the Ark Tablet
p: The Ark Tablet doubles the call, "Wall, wall! Reed wall, reed wall!", and names Atrahasis.

readings.w: C2, one of the two pieces (C1 and C2) of Ipiq-Aya's Old Babylonian copy of Tablet III from Sippar (SEAL Ms. C: BM 78942+78971+80385 (+) MAH 16064)
The Ark Tablet (Douglas Simmonds Collection, provenance unknown; ed. I. Finkel 2014; SEAL files it with the Middle Babylonian versions), lines 1-3
readings.orig: i-ga-ar i-ga-a[r k]i-ki-iš ki-ki-iš / {m}At-ra-am-ḫa-si-i[s] a-na mi-il-ki-ia qú-ul-[ma] / ta-ba-al-lu-uṭ [d]a-ri-iš
readings.en: Wall, wall! Reed wall, reed wall! Atrahasis, pay attention to my counsel, and you will live forever!
readings.plain: Wall, wall! Reed wall, reed wall! Atrahasis, heed my counsel, and you will live forever!

why: The Plain follows Ipiq-Aya's copy, the base text of Tablet III. The Ark Tablet is a separate, shorter version of the flood story with its own wording; it is given here because it fills out the same speech.
b: The Ark Tablet names Atrahasis inside the speech to the wall, which spoils the pretense that Enki is only talking to a wall, and promises him life "forever," as Ziusudra and Utnapishtim receive life like the gods in the Sumerian and Gilgamesh versions. Ipiq-Aya's copy keeps up the pretense.

t: Keep life alive, or keep it safe
p: Ipiq-Aya's copy says bulliṭ, "keep alive"; the Ark Tablet says šullim, "keep safe, whole."

readings.w: C2, Ipiq-Aya's Old Babylonian copy from Sippar

readings.plain: and keep life safe and whole!

why: The base copy is followed. The meaning is close; the Ark Tablet's verb šullum (related to Hebrew shalom) stresses keeping life unharmed.

p: Ipiq-Aya's copy keeps only "equal." The Ark Tablet has the full line: length and breadth equal.

readings.orig: eleppam(MÁ) te-ep-pu-šu e-[ṣ]e-er-ši-ma / e-ṣe-er-ti ki-[i]p-pa-tim / lu mi-it-ḫa-ar ši-id-da-[š]a ù pu-u[s-sa]
readings.en: the boat you will make, draw it out: a plan of a circle; let its length and its breadth be equal
readings.plain: its length and its width must be equal

why: The Plain gives only what survives in the base copy. The Ark Tablet's line is a different version, not a restoration of this copy, though both say the boat's sides are equal; the next surviving word in Ipiq-Aya's copy, "a circle" (10:21), matches the Ark Tablet's round plan.

a: the wild creatures of the open country.
t: Two by two in the Ark Tablet
p: The Ark Tablet says the wild animals went into the boat "two by two," like Genesis.

readings.w: C1, Ipiq-Aya's Old Babylonian copy from Sippar
readings.en: the moving creatures of the steppe
readings.plain: the wild creatures of the open country.

readings.en: and the wild animals from the steppe, two by two, into the boat ...
readings.plain: the wild creatures of the open country, two by two.

why: The base copy is followed; it does not say how many of each animal went in. The Ark Tablet's ša-na, "two each," is a separate version's wording, and the following signs are broken.
b: "Two by two" is the language of Genesis 6:19-20 and 7:9, 15. The Ark Tablet is the only Mesopotamian flood text known to use it. It does not decide whether Genesis borrowed: Genesis also has "seven and seven" of the clean animals (Genesis 7:2), which no Babylonian version has.

a: Pitch was brought, and he sealed his door.
p: In the Ark Tablet the hero tells it himself: "When I went in: seal the frame of her door!"

readings.w: C1, Ipiq-Aya's Old Babylonian copy (third person)
readings.en: pitch was brought; he sealed his door
readings.plain: Pitch was brought, and he sealed his door.

readings.w: The Ark Tablet, lines 59-60 (first person, the hero speaking)
readings.en: when I went in, (I said:) seal the frame of her door!
readings.plain: When I went in, I said, "Seal the frame of her door!"

why: The base copy is followed. The Ark Tablet tells the building and boarding in the hero's own voice, as Utnapishtim does in Gilgamesh XI.

a: that Anu had hung up long before:
p: The tablet's signs here are garbled; SEAL corrects two words. The sense "hung up" depends on it.

readings.w: C1 as edited by SEAL, with corrections
readings.en: which Anu had hung up in front of former time (or: in front of the ancient ones)
readings.plain: that Anu had hung up long before:

readings.w: C1 as the signs are written (ŠU and MA where SEAL reads lu and lu)
readings.en: which Anu ... in front of ... (no clear sense)

why: Read as written the signs make no clear word; SEAL's correction gives the verb alālu, "to hang up," which fits the necklace that follows (12:27-28) and the matching line in Gilgamesh XI, where Anu made the goddess's jewels.
